title: Death close
hookLine: sixty days facing the end, to live better now

cards: This block has run sixty days. It opened with the oldest question, and a page where you wrote what you think.

Since then: Socrates weighing sleep against a journey, the Buddha's last words, a boy waiting at Death's door, a mourner's prayer that never mentions death, Martha and the resurrection, an atom's weight of good, Zhuangzi's skull, marigolds and lanterns, hospice nurses, tea, an ethical will.
Today the block closes on the point the whole thing was for.

teach.b: First, number our days, a psalm this block already sat with once: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." The counting isn't there to frighten. It's there to make a heart wise, now.

Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond, and he said why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived."
Death is in the sentence, but the sentence is about living.
Third, back to the day. Marcus, in his notebook, wrote of passing each day as if it were the last, neither frantic nor numb, so the day in front of him would be done well.
Different homes, one direction of travel: the end looked at squarely, then the face turned back toward today.
Fourth, live, then. It isn't a promise about what happens after; the traditions differ on that, and the block leaves them differing.
It's what these teachers did once they had looked at death: they went back into the day, a little more awake.

how: People on many paths keep death in view as a way of living more fully: Psalm 90 is read in Jewish and Christian worship, Stoics wrote notes to themselves about the end, and some readers return to Thoreau's Walden for its call to live deliberately.

practice: Step outside if you can, or stand at an open window, and breathe in this air, today's air. Breathe out and let the sixty days be finished; there's nothing to conclude.
Let your eyes find one living thing out there, a tree, a bird, a person walking past, and stay with it, saying the line silently if you like: live, then.
